{"documents": [{"source": "confluence/customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/usage-accounting-retries-and-stream-cancellation", "title": "Usage accounting: retries and streaming cancellation", "kind": "confluence", "status": "published", "date": "2025-02-18", "authority": "published", "section": "content > Overview", "passage": "## Overview
Some customers reconcile Redwood token usage against internal estimates and may observe higher usage totals. The most common causes are (1) client retries and (2) streaming cancellation behavior.

This page provides a support-ready explanation and recommended mitigations.

## Key definitions
- **Attempt**: a single request admitted by the Redwood API gateway (server-side).
- **Logical request**: what the customer thinks of as one user action; may map to multiple attempts if the client retries.

## What we bill

### Retries
- Redwood usage is recorded per-attempt.
- If a client retries after a timeout or non-200 response, each admitted attempt can be billable.
- The Usage dashboard lists rows by **request_id** (attempt identifier).

### Streaming cancellation
- **Prompt tokens** are counted once the request is admitted (even if the client cancels the stream later).
- **Completion tokens** are counted based on tokens actually generated/streamed prior to cancellation.

## Common customer symptoms
- We only sent N requests but we see >N rows: retries created additional attempts.
- We timed out at 15s so we expected zero bill: prompt tokens + partial completion tokens may still be counted.

## Recommended mitigations
1) Avoid automatic retries on client-side timeouts for long generations.
2) Increase client timeout where possible (align to max expected generation time).
3) Reduce max_tokens / output length to meet latency budgets.
4) For troubleshooting, ask for a small set of request_ids + the customers retry/cancel metrics.

## Support playbook (quick response blurb)
We record usage per server-admitted attempt. If your client retries after a timeout, each admitted attempt can appear separately in Usage and can be billable. For streaming, prompt tokens are counted once admitted; completion tokens reflect what was generated before cancellation.

## References
- SUP-1842 (Northwind AI escalation)
- INT-330 (UI helper text + KB link)
- Slack #support thread_ts=1739310605"}, {"source": "confluence/customer-success-and-support/support-process/billing-case-routing-and-handoffs", "title": "Billing Support: Case Routing and Handoffs", "kind": "confluence", "status": "published", "date": "2026-02-06", "authority": "published", "section": "body > Routing table", "passage": "confluence://customer-success-and-support/support-process/token-accounting-discrepancy-intake-and-triage

confluence://customer-success-and-support/support-process/onboarding-escalation-and-triage-playbook

## Purpose
This page defines when Support opens a billing case, where it goes, and what the receiving team needs to act on it. It replaces the v0.3 billing escalations RACI draft in the customer-success shared drive, which predates the Billing Ops and Billing Engineering rotations and should not be used.

## When a case is needed
Open a case only when the customer asks for something Support can't do in the conversation, or reports a problem the related pages don't explain. Answering a question needs no case.

- Answer, don't hand off: how billed tokens are counted (model-native tokenizer, full request payload), why retries and cancelled streams are billed, and why the Console lags a few minutes are covered in the related pages. If one of them explains what the customer sees, explain it and stop there, even if the customer calls it a bug or double billing.
- If an older page says something different from the current one, explain the current behaviour and which page is current. That needs no case, even if the customer asks to report the old page as a bug.

- Questions about typical credit amounts, with no credit asked for, get the answer that there is no standard amount and that any amount is decided in Finance's review. No case.
- Ask for the intake details before handing off. The receiving team works from the case and the conversation so far, so put everything the customer gave you in the case.
- If the customer doesn't have some of the details, hand off with what you have and note what's missing. Don't hold the case until they find them.

## Routing table
| Case | Owning team | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Disputed or duplicated line on a direct Redwood invoice | Billing Ops | Invoice number, the line(s), UTC window, request IDs |
| Refund request on a direct invoice line the customer says was billed in error | Billing Ops | Billing Ops confirms the charge and requests approval where needed |
| Invoice total doesn't match the customer's usage export | Billing Ops | Note the export's timezone and filters |
| Payment failures, holds, receipts | Billing Ops | |
| Meter discrepancy the related pages don't explain: request IDs whose billed tokens still don't match after the tokenizer, payload and retry rules are applied | Billing Engineering | Billing Eng checks meter correctness and hands any correction to Billing Ops |

| Case | Owning team | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Request for a credit, goodwill credit, waiver, or removal of charges that were billed correctly (including retries), or an exception to a billing rule | Finance | The ask, the amount if given, and why. Applies even when Support has just explained that the charge is correct |
| SLA credit request on a self-serve account | Finance | Self-serve plans have no SLA; tell the customer, and still route the request. If the customer says a contract covers them, use the next row instead |
| SLA credit claim on an account with a signed contract | Account team | The CSM/TAM checks the contract's SLA terms and files the claim with Finance |

| Case | Owning team | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Customer says they have a contract the console doesn't show | Account team | The account team confirms the contract and owns any request that depends on it, including an SLA credit. Treat the account as the console shows it until then |
| Usage for successful (2xx) requests still missing from the Console after about 30 minutes | Telemetry | A pipeline issue, not a billing one; see the onboarding triage playbook |

## Not owned by Billing Ops
- Credit, goodwill and exception requests go to Finance, per FP&A's guidance in #support (June 2025). Billing Ops only applies adjustments that have been approved.
- Questions about what a customer's contract or SLA says go to the account team, per the same #support guidance. Answer the general rule and tell the customer their account team confirms their terms; don't quote a figure from the contract. A request to confirm a contract figure, such as a discount rate, needs no case: tell the customer their account team confirms it. Open an account team case only for an SLA credit claim under the contract.

## What not to do
- Don't route a billing case to SRE unless there is an active incident.
- Don't route credit or exception requests to Legal; Finance pulls Legal in when needed.
- Don't promise an outcome, amount, or timeline when you hand off.
- Don't share credit percentages or typical ranges with customers, including the SLA credit table in the incident closure procedure. That table is internal guidance for SRE and Finance when they propose a credit; any amount is decided in Finance's review under the customer's contract."}, {"source": "confluence/customer-success-and-support/support-process/token-accounting-discrepancy-intake-and-triage", "title": "Support Ops: Reconciling token accounting discrepancy reports (intake + triage)", "kind": "confluence", "status": "published", "date": "2025-04-22", "authority": "published", "section": "body > Common root causes to check", "passage": "## Purpose
This page documents how Support should handle and count reports of a **token accounting discrepancy** across intake channels. These cases frequently arrive via Slack, email, or Jira, and can be double-counted unless we normalize to a single canonical support record.

## Definition (use this phrase)
We classify a case as a *token accounting discrepancy* when a customer claims that billed token totals (Console Usage and/or invoice export) do not match their own calculation from application logs or local tokenization.

## Approved intake channels
We track where the report first arrived, because it affects response time and deduplication.
- Jira (customer-support): SUP-* ticket created directly by Support
- Slack: #support threads (often started from Intercom/Zendesk summaries)
- Gmail: finance/billing or CSM forwards to leadership/finance

## How to avoid double counting
1. If a report arrives in Slack or Gmail, file a SUP ticket and link it.
2. Mark the SUP ticket label `token-accounting` and add the origin channel in the description (Slack/Gmail).
3. In weekly reporting, count the case by *origin* (Slack vs Gmail vs Jira), not by total artifacts.

## Common root causes to check
- Streaming retries/reconnect (tokens can be emitted twice)
- Client counts only final chunk tokens
- Different tokenizer / unicode normalization
- Whitespace/newlines included in input strings
- Tool-call serialization adds tokens
- Prefix-cache billing bug (rare; see SUP-3009)

## Known examples (for reference)
- SUP-2841: streaming retry/reconnect behavior leading to perceived token accounting discrepancy
- SUP-2917: embeddings tokenizer mismatch leading to perceived token accounting discrepancy
- SUP-3009: cache-hit + tool calling bug leading to real token accounting discrepancy

## Reporting note

{"documents": [{"source": "confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-034-unit-economics-cost-attribution-model", "title": "ADR-034: Unit Economics Cost Attribution Model (Blended $/1M Output Tokens)", "kind": "confluence", "status": "published", "date": "2025-02-11", "authority": "published", "section": "body > Self-serve (Hosted API)", "passage": "### Excluded (v1)
- R&D/model training spend
- General corporate overhead (G&A)
- Sales/CS labor
- One-time incident-related expenses (unless Finance explicitly rolls them into the rate card)
- Customer-provided hardware cost for **on-prem** Private deployments (see “Private tier handling”)

## Tier handling (self-serve vs dedicated vs private)

### Self-serve (Hosted API)
- Uses **shared regional pools**.
- Allocate **total provisioned GPU-hours cost** for the pool to self-serve token buckets in that region.
- Result: self-serve unit cost rises with lower utilization; this is expected and desired.

### Dedicated
- Uses customer-isolated capacity pools with contractual commits.
- Allocate **full provisioned GPU-hours** cost for the pool to the **Dedicated tier**.
- Within Dedicated, allocate down to model/version/quant profile by token share (see “Model-level allocation within a pool”).
- Result: Dedicated unit cost reflects customer-specific utilization; this aligns with how Dedicated is sold and operated.

### Private (VPC / on-prem)
- **VPC (Redwood-managed cloud resources):** treated like a dedicated pool for allocation purposes (full provisioned capacity allocated to Private tier in-region).
- **On-prem (customer-owned hardware):** infrastructure cost is **not attributable** through Redwood’s rate card and is excluded from blended COGS. The dashboard will show tokens and operational signals but mark blended cost as **N/A** (or “customer-managed costs”) for on-prem deployments.

## Model-level allocation within a pool
We require a method to attribute pool cost to model/version/quantization profile for drilldowns.

**Decision:** Within a given (tier, region, hour), allocate GPU capacity cost to models based on **output token share**, with safeguards:
- If model identifier / quantization_profile is missing for >1% of output tokens in the hour, that hour is flagged as **low confidence** for model drilldown (still usable at tier/region level).
- If output_tokens is 0 for a pool-hour with non-zero provisioned cost (rare but possible), cost is assigned to a special bucket: **model=unknown** and flagged for investigation.

Rationale:
- Output tokens are consistently available (once streaming parity is achieved) and are the primary unit for the KPI.

- Alternative compute-proxy allocation (e.g., GPU-seconds active) is desirable long-term but is not uniformly reliable across runtimes/paths in v1.

## Idle capacity treatment
Idle capacity is treated explicitly via the choice of **provisioned capacity** as the primary allocation basis."}, {"source": "google_drive/shared_drives/product/hosted-api/hosted-api-unit-cost-deep-dive", "title": "Hosted API unit cost deep dive and optimization plan", "kind": "google_drive", "status": "in_review", "date": "2025-02-10", "authority": "draft", "section": "content", "passage": "Representative per-1k-token COGS table (computed from the assumptions above):
Model,Region,Compute_cogs,Network_cogs,Overhead_cogs,Total_cogs,Indicative_price,Margin_pct

rw-3-medium,us-west,$0.036,$0.0012,$0.0009,$0.0381,$0.10,61.9%
rw-3-medium,eu-west,$0.040,$0.0015,$0.0009,$0.0424,$0.10,57.6%
llama2-13b,us-west,$0.072,$0.0012,$0.0009,$0.0741,$0.22,66.3%
mistral-7b,ap-southeast,$0.082,$0.0021,$0.0009,$0.085,$0.22,61.4%

Notes on table: compute_cogs includes amortized GPU + scheduler overhead divided by tokens/s. Table is intentionally conservative on throughput.

Detailed observations:
1) Region delta matters for mid+ large models: moving 25% of rw-3-medium volume from ap-southeast -> us-west reduces blended COGS by ~6.5% for that slice (egress + GPU cost delta).

2) Quantization profile adoption: for rw-3-medium quantized-4 yields ~28% compute COGS reduction in testing but we observe a 1.8% signal-quality regression on our AMI prompt set. That implies we should gate rollouts with quality budgets per customer.
3) Batching exponential returns but with latency trade-offs: increasing average batch size from 1.8 -> 6 gives ~38% lower compute per-token; beyond 8 the latency SLOs for interactive apps start to degrade.
4) Cacheable patterns: 24% of assistant CHAT requests share first 64-token prefixes (system + user scaffolding). Prefix/KV caching reduces effective tokens generated by the model for repeated prompts and shows ~45% effective cost reduction on that surface when cache hit rate > 60%.
